query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. Al seems to have a minor effect on both Ni and Co, both of which are the weakest oxidizing component and it seems to have no effects on both unoxidized and oxidized states. We infer that Al addition does not have significant electronic interaction with Co and Ni (Fig. 4h, i), this is shown as their oxidation behavior remains the same in Fig. 4d. Figure 4j summarizes these interactions where Mn-Al tends to have the strongest interaction and both Ni and Co being the weakest. This study uncovers the oxidation process in compositionally complex alloys. Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). We chose a relatively low oxidation temperature to prevent phase transformation in the alloy, focusing solely on examining the oxidation process in the super-saturated alloy condition. decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has been focused on understanding their mechanical properties, microstructure, and degradation behavior under various conditions. Earlier studies have investigated the effects of composition, processing, and heat treatment on the properties of these alloys. Recently, there has been a shift towards designing alloys with specific properties, such as high strength and ductility, using computational models and machine learning techniques. The use of additive manufacturing techniques, such as laser powder bed fusion, has also been explored to produce complex components with minimal machining processes.
decision.unsolved: The degradation behavior of high-entropy alloys under elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases is not well understood, and a mechanistic hypothesis that explains this behavior is still lacking. The effects of synergistic elemental effects, composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing on the degradation behavior of these alloys are not fully understood.
decision.why: To investigate the microstructural evolution and degradation behavior of the Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy under elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases, and to gain insights into the mechanistic hypothesis governing this behavior. This technique will allow for real-time observation of the microstructural changes and degradation processes, providing valuable information for understanding the underlying mechanisms.
